extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and writers composing in English (practitioners and critics of poetic and dramatic writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing poetry and drama in English, covering choice of dramatic moment, genre integrity, diction, rhetorical figures, versification, and the moral/educational ends of verse. Targets writers aiming to write effective tragedies, comedies, and lyrical verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the proper point of action (show, don't tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: A playwright should represent the most effective moment of the action rather than recount long backstory; begin where the action to be represented best exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Polydorus example: a tragedy-writer would begin with the delivery of the child rather than sailing over years of travel; Euripides begins with finding the body and leaves the rest to be told, which is an inferior method. "Where, now, would one of our tragedy-writers begin, but with the delivery of the child?... But where doth Euripides? Even with the finding of the body; leaving the rest to be told by the spirit of Polydorus." (anti-pattern: stretching the represented action so that important parts are merely narrated rather than shown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proper genre integrity (avoid mongrel tragi-comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix the high and low improperly — avoid thrusting clowns into majestic matters where neither tragedy nor comedy is properly obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises plays "mingling kings and clowns, not because the matter so carrieth it, but thrust in the clown by head and shoulders to play a part in majestical matters" leading to neither admiration nor proper sportfulness. Notes that true tragi-comedy is rare and when mishandled yields scurrility unworthy of chaste ears. (anti-pattern: matching "horn-pipes and funerals"; forced clowning in high scenes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy must combine delight with teaching, not mere laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of comedy is not laughter alone but "that delightful teaching which is the end of poesy" — comedy should instruct as well as amuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "all the end of the comical part be not upon such scornful matters as stir laughter only, but mix with it that delightful teaching which is the end of poesy." Acceptable comic subjects are those that produce both delight and moral or instructive insight (examples: a busy loving courtier, a heartless Thraso, a self-wise school-master). (scoring note: measure comic passages by whether they teach as well as provoke laughter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid laughing at the miserable or morally execrable (ethical limits of comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not base laughter on things that are miserable or execrable — ridicule should not target the pitiable or condemnable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly forbidden (cites Aristotle): "they stir laughter in sinful things, which are rather execrable than ridiculous; or in miserable, which are rather to be pitied than scorned." Examples of anti-patterns: making fun of a wretched beggar, jesting at strangers for imperfect English. Quoted maxim and Latin line demonstrating the harshness of ridiculing the poor. (evaluation: comedy loses moral worth if it targets victims rather than follies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose comic targets that teach (ridicule folly, not misfortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer ridiculing affectations, vanity, and folly (e.g., a busy loving courtier, the self-wise school-master) rather than attacking persons for poverty or misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples of desirable comic subjects — characters who exhibit arrogant or foolish behaviour, whose exposure yields "delightful laughter and teaching delightfulness." Contrasts with scurrility and mere buffoonery that teach nothing. (guideline: aim satire at vice/folly, not suffering.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural diction; avoid affected, far-fetched words and painted affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be natural and fit to convey the conceit of the mind; avoid 'honey-flowing matron eloquence', far-fetched or strange words, and the appearance of studied artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against "so far-fetched words, that many seem monsters, but most seem strangers to any poor Englishman" and against "figures and flowers, extremely winter-starved." Advises against imitating rhetorical ornament blindly ('cast sugar and spice upon every dish'). (anti-pattern: prose or verse that sounds like a dictionary or shows off foreign phrases to seem learned.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate classical masters by translation and understanding, not verbatim grafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should 'attentive[ly] translate' and make classical figures and phrasing their own, rather than swallowing them whole from handbooks or phrase-lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "I could wish the diligent imitators of Tully and Demosthenes... did not so much keep Nizolian paper-books of their figures and phrases, as by attentive translation, as it were, devour them whole, and make them wholly theirs." (anti-pattern: carrying lists of figures into one's work and thereby producing artificial, unpersuasive style.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hide art: technique should serve nature and persuasion, not display itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Artifice should be used to hide art — do not 'use art to show art'; the best practice persuades by seeming natural rather than ostentatious technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts the courtier who, by practice, fits nature and thus 'doth according to art, though not by art', with the scholar who 'using art to show art... flieth from nature, and indeed abuseth art.' Persuasion (the chief mark of oratory and poetic effect) arises when technique is subordinate to natural expression. (evaluation: effective writing reads as natural and persuasive rather than self-consciously ornate.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical figures and similitudes sparingly and with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Similitudes (metaphors, comparisons) exist to explain to a willing hearer; when overused they become tedious and distract from the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The force of a similitude... when that is done, the rest is a most tedious prattling, rather overswaying the memory from the purpose..." Criticises theft of multitudes of similitudes from herbalists and bestiary lore to dress every conceit. (anti-pattern: piling dozens of stock similes that swamp the idea instead of clarifying it.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply rhetorical devices in appropriate contexts (avoid misapplied repetition and ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices effective in one genre or setting (e.g., oratory repetition) may be inappropriate elsewhere (e.g., a familiar epistle or pulpit); match device to context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tully's figure of repetition suits a thunderbolt oratory but becomes excessive in a familiar letter or the pulpit; repetition and delicate cadences should be used where they fit the gravity and purpose of the speech. "They have made me think of the sophister..." (evaluation: judge rhetorical forms by contextual fit and persuasive effect.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and exploit English's strengths (compound phrases, accent, caesura)
rubrics_metrics.description: English is particularly apt for certain poetic constructions — compounds of two or three words, precise accentual patterns, and an available caesura — and should be used to advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues English 'is particularly happy in compositions of two or three words together' and praises its suitability for both ancient quantity and modern rhyme. Notes English avoids the cumbersome case/gender/mood inflections of other tongues and has advantages over Italian, Dutch, French, and Spanish in accent and rhyme placement. (practical tip: use English's natural word-combinations and accentual rhythm.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Match versification method to musical and expressive aims (quantity vs rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide between the 'ancient' quantitative versification (quantity of syllables) and the 'modern' accent/rhyme-based method according to musical goals and expressive requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient verse (quantity) is 'more fit for music' and for expressing various passions by well-weighed syllables; the modern (number and rhyme) 'striketh a certain music to the ear' and also achieves sweetness and majesty. "Whether of these be the more excellent, would bear many speeches... Truly the English... is fit for both sorts." (guideline: choose the system that serves music and passion intended.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to accent, caesura, and rhyme-types in English verse
rubrics_metrics.description: When composing in English, observe accent placement, the cæsura (breathing-place), and the available rhyme types (masculine, feminine, sdrucciola) to create proper verse rhythm and musicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains English precisely observes accent and often has a cæsura; gives examples of masculine (last-syllable) and feminine/sdrucciola (penultimate/ante-penultimate) rhyme distinctions, with language comparisons (Italian, French, Spanish) and English examples: 'due/true' (masc.), 'father/rather' (fem.), 'motion/potion' (sdrucciola). (practical tip: exploit these rhyme types and the cæsura for variety and musical effect.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for poetry's twin ends: delight and moral/civil instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should produce delight and also carry teaching—moral, civic, or philosophical content—so that pleasure is coupled with instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States poetry is 'full of virtue, breeding delightfulness' and that songs and sonnets could be used to sing praises of immortal goodness and God. Urges readers not to scorn poets because poetry contains 'many mysteries... which of purpose were written darkly' and that reading poetry can make one a better person (citations of Scaliger, Bembus, Clauserus). (evaluation: measure poetry by whether it delights and imparts wisdom or moral value.)
